newsitem.title: LEBANON: Executive's disappearance poses question in Lebanon.
newsitem.headline: Executive's disappearance poses question in Lebanon.

text.p: A Jordanian hotel executive in Beirut returned home safely at the weekend after a three-week disappearance that raised questions about the safety of foreigners in Lebanon.

The disappearance of Derar al-Karmi, financial controller at the Marriott Hotel, damaged Beirut's ties with Jordan whose ambassador indicated the Palestinian-born Jordanian was taken from the hotel by Syrian intelligence agents.
Before Karmi reappeared on Saturday, Jordan protested to the Lebanese foreign ministry that the Beirut authorities had failed to answer Amman's official enquiries.

Karmi, a longtime employee of the U.S.-owned Marriott group, was taken from the recently opened hotel on January 3 by three men in civilian clothes. Jordanian Ambassador Fakhry Abou Taleb told reporters last week that as Karmi left, he whispered to a colleague "mukhabarat" (intelligence officers).
Nothing more was heard for three weeks. Marriott executives in Beirut and Lebanon's Prosecutor-General Adnan Addoum said they had no idea who was holding Karmi or why or where.

When Karmi returned to his wife and four children at 9.30 p.m. on January 25 after 25 days, he was said to have lost a lot of weight but was otherwise in good condition. He and Marriott executives refused to say what had happened.
"He's not saying anything...The Marriott doesn't want to say anything either...He doesn't want to meet the press," a hotel official said.

The disappearance coincided with Washington's six-monthly review of its ban on U.S. travel to Lebanon imposed in 1985 after a U.S. airliner was hijacked to Beirut and an American passenger on board was murdered at Beirut airport.

Lebanese authorities insist each time the ban comes up for review it is safe for U.S. citizens and airlines to return to Beirut. Karmi was still missing when the U.S. State Department announced on January 17 it was again extending the ban.

Nobody in Beirut believes the incident was a return to the 1980s when shadowy Moslem groups like Islamic Jihad seized foreigners and killed them or held them hostage for years, giving Beirut the reputation of the kidnap capital of the world.

A Lebanese political analyst who asked not to be identified said he believed Karmi's disappearance was intended to send a message to Jordan, and also to Saudi Arabia which is the chief backer of Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri.

"But this will have been registered in Washington. I think there is a fear there that foreigners in Lebanon, especially Americans, could be used as bargaining chips in some regional squabbles," the analyst added.

The prosecutor-general at first avowed total ignorance but then said Karmi had been detained on orders of Lebanese military judicial authorities. But he said he did not know where or why he was being held and would not say if he was in Lebanon or Syria.

Beirut newspapers speculated Karmi was being questioned about a December attack on Syrian workers north of Beirut or a bus bombing in Damascus that killed 11 people. Syria has 35,000 troops in Lebanon and is the country's main power broker.

Reports from Jordan quoted Marriott officials there as saying the Beirut hotel had had difficult relations with Syrian troops billeted in a derelict building beside the hotel. But Marriott officials in Beirut dismissed the reports in private, saying relations with the Syrian unit had always been good.
